form.2. SHORT COURSE DESCRIPTION: This course examines modern AI-native software development, where developers collaborate with increasingly capable coding agents. It covers how to define intent, provide effective context, structure development workflows, and coordinate AI tools. Students gain practical experience designing and evaluating agent-assisted software development processes.
form.3. TOPICS / CONTENT AREAS:
Treatment of this list: starting hypotheses — may add/drop/reorder with justification
A. AI-Native Development: AI-assisted coding, coding agents, developer workflows

B. Agentic Software Engineering: MCP, agent skills, tool use, context engineering

C. Specification & Planning: spec-driven development, requirements to executable specifications

D. Software Development Workflows: loop engineering, iterative development, software factories

E. Engineering Practice: automated testing, evaluation, deployment, reliability

F. Practical Development: hands-on coding, projects, emerging developer tools
form.4. COURSE INTENT:
Central question the course answers: How can software developers effectively
design and operate development workflows in which humans and AI agents
collaboratively build reliable software?

Pedagogical emphasis: Practical, workflow-oriented understanding through
hands-on development and experimentation.

This course should NOT become:
- A general introduction to AI or machine learning
- A traditional programming course
- A purely theoretical treatment of large language models
form.5. TARGET STUDENTS:
Programmes: B.Tech. CSE
Year: 3rd/4th year
Assumed background: Strong programming and software development fundamentals;
familiarity with advanced programming and basic software engineering concepts.

Lab required: Yes — hands-on coding and development activities

Available infrastructure: Student development machines, access to
AI coding tools/APIs, software development environments, and TA support.
form.12. ASSESSMENT PREFERENCES:
Preferred components: Practical assignments, hands-on coding exercises,
project-based evaluation, and a final project.

Components to avoid: none

AI-assisted development practices rather than primarily testing theory.

programme_pos.text: Engineering knowledge: Apply the knowledge of mathematics, science, engineering fundamentals and an engineering specialization to the solution of complex engineering problems.

Problem analysis: Identify, formulate, review research literature, and analyze complex engineering problems reaching substantiated conclusions using first principles of mathematics, natural sciences, and engineering sciences.

Design/development of solutions: Design solutions for complex engineering problems and design system components or processes that meet the specified needs with appropriate consideration for the public health and safety, and the cultural, societal, and environmental considerations.

Conduct investigations of complex problems: Use research-based knowledge and research methods including design of experiments, analysis and interpretation of data, and synthesis of the information to provide valid conclusions.

Modern tool usage: Create, select, and apply appropriate techniques, resources, and modern engineering and IT tools including prediction and modeling to complex engineering activities with an understanding of the limitations.

The engineer and society: Apply reasoning informed by the contextual knowledge to assess societal, health, safety, legal and cultural issues and the consequent responsibilities relevant to the professional engineering practice.

Environment and sustainability: Understand the impact of the professional engineering solutions in societal and environmental contexts, and demonstrate the knowledge of, and need for sustainable development.
Ethics: Apply ethical principles and commit to professional ethics and responsibilities and norms of the engineering practice.
Individual and team work: Function effectively as an individual, and as a member or leader in diverse teams, and in multidisciplinary settings.

Communication: Communicate effectively on complex engineering activities with the engineering community and with society at large, such as, being able to comprehend and write effective reports and design documentation, make effective presentations, and give and receive clear instructions.

Project management and finance: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the engineering and management principles and apply these to one’s own work, as a member and leader in a team, to manage projects and in multidisciplinary environments.
Life-long learning: Recognize the need for, and have the preparation and ability to engage in independent and life-long learning in the broadest context of technological change.
Understanding of theoretical foundations and limits of computing.
Understanding of computing at different levels of abstraction including circuits and computer architecture, operating systems, algorithms, and applications.
Ability to adapt established models, techniques, algorithms, data structures, etc. for efficiently solving new problems.
Ability to design, implement, and evaluate computer based system or application to meet the desired needs using modern tools and methodologies.
Understanding and ability to use advanced techniques and tools in different areas of computing.
Understanding of foundational topics in Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, and Machine Learning.
Understanding of theoretical foundations and limits of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning.
Ability to design and implement algorithms and data structures for efficiently solving new problems.
Ability to model and analyze a variety of problems using appropriate mathematical/computational and AI concepts.
Ability of apply and develop AI algorithms to transform large amount of data into intelligent decisions and/or behavior.
An understanding of the impact of AI based solutions in an economic, societal, and environment context.
An ability to independently carry out research /investigation and development work to solve practical problems
An ability to write and present a substantial technical report/document

narrative.course_description: This course examines AI-native software development, focusing on how developers collaborate with AI coding agents within structured software engineering workflows. Intended for third- and fourth-year B.Tech. Computer Science and Engineering students, the course addresses the core challenges of defining developer intent, managing context resources, and coordinating agentic tools. Students learn to configure agent workspaces using the Model Context Protocol, design executable software specifications from ambiguous requirements, instrument human-agent development loops to diagnose context failure modes, and establish continuous verification pipelines using synthetic defect injection. Additionally, students evaluate software quality metrics to refactor agent-generated technical debt across multi-turn workflows. The course is not a general introduction to artificial intelligence or basic programming, but a specialized study of collaborative human-AI software engineering. Instruction is delivered through a combination of lectures, tutorial sessions, and hands-on laboratory work, culminating in practical project development.
narrative.sequencing_rationale: Building upon foundational software engineering and unit testing concepts from CSE201, the course begins with setting up agent workspaces and protocol adapters (M1). Students advance to specification-driven prompt engineering and code synthesis (M2). With operational context established, the curriculum progresses to diagnosing context degradation in agentic loops (M3), followed by automated continuous verification pipelines (M4). It culminates in evaluating long-term software quality and architectural refactoring strategies (M5).
narrative.assessment_rationale: The assessment structure matches the course's practical and analytical goals. Hands-on assignments (20%) and a continuous software project (25%) directly evaluate practical skills in configuring context protocols, synthesizing code, and building automated verification pipelines (CO1, CO2, CO4). Quizzes (10%), mid-semester (20%), and end-semester examinations (25%) evaluate theoretical understanding of context failure diagnostics and quantitative maintainability metrics (CO3, CO5).
narrative.positioning_rationale: Unlike CSE594A, which focuses on foundational agentic reasoning architectures for algorithmic and mathematical problem solving, this course addresses the full software development lifecycle. It specifically concentrates on specification-driven development, Model Context Protocol integration, automated testing pipelines, and software maintainability metrics within multi-turn human-agent workflows.
